methods.label: Tracking the cube faces
methods.explanation:
Track which cube face each square would occupy, since the five squares must cover five different faces. Call the three original squares in the upper row \(P,Q,R\), from left to right, and call the original square below \(P\) square \(S\).

Place \(P\) on the front of a cube. Folding along the shared edges puts \(Q\) on the right, \(R\) on the back, and \(S\) on the bottom. The two unused faces are the top and the left. Once these placements are fixed, the shared attachment edge determines where an additional square must go.

Positions \(5,6,7\), above the three upper squares, each fold onto the top face. Positions \(4,8,9\) each fold onto the left face: position \(4\) continues the strip around the cube, while positions \(8\) and \(9\) attach beside the front and bottom faces. Thus all six of these positions give five distinct cube faces.

Position \(1\), beyond the bottom square, folds onto the back face already occupied by \(R\). Position \(3\), below the back square, folds onto the bottom face already occupied by \(S\). Position \(2\) completes a \(2\times2\) block, whose four squares share one corner. This cannot become a cube corner, where only three faces meet.

These cases account for all nine indicated positions, each once. Therefore \(6\) positions work, choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses elementary spatial reasoning, right-angle folds, and an exhaustive check of the nine positions.
